newsitem.title: USA: Farm groups oppose CFTC "pro market" reform.
newsitem.headline: Farm groups oppose CFTC "pro market" reform.

text.p: The American Farm Bureau Federation, several major farm groups and Cargill Inc said on Thursday they opposed legislation that would create an unregulated "professional market" in U.S. futures trading.

In testimony before a House Agriculture subcommittee, the agriculture groups said the proposed legislation to reform the Commodity Futures Trading Commission went too far in reducing government regulation.

"Farmers and ranchers, regardless of whether they directly utilize futures markets, will be severely impacted if a lack of market integrity disrupts the price discovery process," said Bryce Neidig, who represented the American Farm Bureau Federation, the American Soybean Association, the National Association of Wheat Growers and seven other farm groups.

Legislation sponsored by Rep. Thomas Ewing (R-Ill) would effectively strip the CFTC of much of its power by creating a so-called professional market free from government regulation. The professional market would include about 90 percent of the U.S. futures traded, according to industry estimates.

The proposed professional markets exemption "conjures up an image of the 'big boys' playing by a different set of rules -- or no rules -- in a 'back room'," testified Ryland Utlaut, vice president of the National Corn Growers Association.
Even if agricultural futures were excluded from the professional markets, liquidity would be lost as speculators move to the unregulated markets, he said.
The corn growers group and others urged the CFTC to work with the U.S. exchanges to find a middle ground.
The U.S. exchanges have pressed for reforms, contending they need less government regulation to remain competitive with overseas futures exchanges.
Cargill, one of the nation's biggest agricultural processors, said in written testimony that a professional market would create a "splintered" market that could shake public confidence.
"Removing a significant segment of the market from such oversight will undermine the public trust and reduce the value of the exchanges and the instruments traded on them," Cargill said.
Similar legislation is pending before a Senate Agriculture subcommittee.
In earlier testimony this week, the Securities and Exchange Commission expressed concern about the legislation and the Federal Reserve urged the exchanges and the CFTC to try to fashion a compromise.
